title: Asian Stocks Hold Firm as AI Rebound Offsets Oil, Fed Hike Fears
excerpt: Asian equities steadied on Tuesday as a tech rebound driven by calls to slow AI development balanced pressure from surging oil prices, a 10-year Treasury yield at 5%, and expectations of a Fed rate hike this week.
body:
• Asian equities steadied on Tuesday as a rebound in AI-linked software and technology shares offset pressure from surging oil prices and rising bond yields.
  • The Federal Reserve begins a two-day meeting with markets pricing in a roughly 90% chance of a 25-basis-point rate hike, which would be the first US increase since mid-2023.
  • The 10-year US Treasury yield touched 5% for the first time since 2023, while the Bank of Japan is widely expected to lift rates to 1.25% on Friday.
  • Brent crude held above $107 a barrel after attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure knocked the kingdom's East-West pipeline offline.

Asian stocks held their ground on Tuesday as a rebound in artificial-intelligence-linked shares blunted the drag from surging oil prices and climbing bond yields, with investors braced for a Federal Reserve meeting that could deliver the first US interest-rate hike in more than three years.

Trading was choppy across the region. A rally in software and services names following a weekend call by leading AI executives to slow the pace of frontier AI development helped steady indexes even as semiconductor stocks stayed soft, mirroring Monday's split session on Wall Street, where chip stocks dropped while software jumped.

AI pause talk steadies tech shares

The shift in tech sentiment followed an essay published early Saturday by Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," in which he urged AI companies to deliberately moderate how fast they improve model capabilities. The call won rare public backing from OpenAI's Sam Altman and Elon Musk, and, according to reports, Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis.

Investors read a slower AI arms race as a near-term reprieve for margins across the technology supply chain. Asian semiconductor stocks remained under pressure, but software and IT services names advanced, lifting the region's tech-heavy benchmarks off their lows.

Central banks back in tightening mode

The Federal Open Market Committee begins its two-day meeting later on Tuesday, with markets pricing in a roughly 90% chance of a 25-basis-point hike on Wednesday, according to Reuters. It would be the Fed's first increase since mid-2023, and Morgan Stanley expects a second hike in December.

"We now expect the Fed to hike twice this year, in September and December. At this stage, failing to back up words with action could put the credibility of the institution at risk."

— Michael Feroli, chief US economist at JPMorgan

Overnight, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield touched 5% for the first time since 2023, while Germany's 10-year yield climbed above 3.51%, its highest since 2009. Japan's 10-year yield popped back to 3% as the Bank of Japan is widely expected to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points to 1.25% at the end of its own two-day meeting on Friday, which would mark a 31-year high, and signal more tightening ahead. Policymakers have been seeking to shore up the yen after intervention helped steer the currency away from a 40-year low.

Prashant Newnaha, senior rates strategist at TD Securities, said 10-year yields above 5% are inevitable for as long as oil sustains above $100, calling the August inflation data "the most important print for the Fed and markets so far this year." Analysts at JPMorgan expect eight of the nine developed-market central banks they cover, including the Fed, the Bank of Japan and the European Central Bank, to raise rates between now and year-end.

Oil keeps inflation risk alive

Brent crude futures traded around $107 a barrel after a drone attack late last week knocked Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline offline. The 750-mile pipeline had been moving 4 to 5 million barrels a day, or 4% to 5% of global supply, to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing the kingdom to bypass the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

Yemen's Houthis added to the pressure with fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia on Monday, while commodity vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dropped to fewer than 10 transits a day over the weekend from a 10-day average of 14, raising concerns over a route that carried about one-fifth of global oil supplies before the US-Iran war began in February.

Diaspora Angle

For investors across the Indian diaspora, the mix of 5% Treasury yields and elevated oil is a double hit: higher US borrowing costs pull capital away from emerging-market equities, while costlier fuel feeds inflation back home in India.

What's Next

The Fed's decision on Wednesday and the Bank of Japan's move on Friday will set the tone for the rest of September. Traders are also watching whether the AI slowdown talk translates into changed capital-spending guidance from big tech, and whether Saudi Arabia can restart partial pipeline operations within days as reported.
